title: After a Record Loss, Leopold Aschenbrenner Is Still Betting Everything on A.I.
excerpt: “Next year is the last year that anything in modern life still feels a little normal,”Aschenbrenner, an investor and an A.I. prophet, says. Stephen Witt reports on the vanguard of the A.I. revolution.
content_html:
Leopold Aschenbrenner, the twenty-five-year-old manager of Situational Awareness LP, a San Francisco hedge fund, has crammed a lot into a quarter century. Born in Germany, he matriculated at Columbia University as a fifteen-year-old. There, he read the great books and joined the debate society. A forty-four-page economics paper he wrote at seventeen was considered Ph.D.-quality work by leading figures in the field. Aschenbrenner graduated, at nineteen, as the school’s valedictorian, and went to seek his fortune in Silicon Valley, where he witnessed, encouraged, and perhaps triggered an ongoing series of spectacular explosions: financial, social, technological, and more.

From late 2024 to mid-2026, Situational Awareness reported returns of more than a thousand per cent, mostly through investments in the A.I. industry. Then, this summer, it blew up, suffering one of the largest trading losses in American stock-market history. About two-thirds of its value was wiped out—but such was the magnitude of Aschenbrenner’s previous gains that Situational Awareness’s returns were still positive for the year.

I met with Aschenbrenner recently at his firm’s offices, near San Francisco’s South Park. The neighborhood was cozy, and I imagined viewing it from an isometric 2-D perspective, as in a world-building game, with little pawns zipping around on e-scooters and the latest trillion-dollar idea indicated by the appearance of an exclamation mark over someone’s head. It was Election Day, but no one in the cafés surrounding the park seemed to notice. The talk was of money—who got in early and who was oversubscribed, who was entering stealth mode and who was exiting it, who got what in the cap table and who missed out. All this was interrupted by little sips of espresso from biodegradable cups.

Situational Awareness’s offices are large and airy; after clearing three security checks, I was seated across from Aschenbrenner at a twenty-two-foot-long conference table. He is tall and a little gangly, with facial features that seem to have been exaggerated for emphasis. His nose and ears are large, his mouth toothy and wide, and he wears his dark-blond hair in a part.

Conversation with Aschenbrenner resembles a formal lecture; you expect, at the end, to be graded on your understanding of what he’s said. When he’s making an especially salient point, his eyebrows raise suggestively above his pale-blue eyes. “We live in a slightly more anarchic world than I expected,” he told me.

Aschenbrenner’s big idea is that the world has not yet grasped the implications of the A.I. revolution. “Next year—that is, calendar year 2027—we will see A.I. accelerate between two and five times faster than anything we have seen so far,” he said. “Next year is the last year that anything in modern life still feels a little normal.” Aschenbrenner has held this view for some time, having explained his insights in 2024, in a long essay titled “Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead.” He predicted that by 2027 spending on A.I. infrastructure would rival the entire U.S. defense budget, that A.I. companies would find themselves targeted by Chinese spies, that traditional software firms would struggle as A.I. automated their work, and that A.I. would outperform even Ph.D.s at intellectual tasks.

All this has occurred, and what in financial circles has become known as the “Leopold trade”—buying shares in data-center suppliers and betting against vulnerable software stocks—has been profitable. And yet Aschenbrenner’s most striking prediction has not yet come to pass: that A.I. itself will automate A.I. research, leading to an explosion in superintelligence. It was maybe for this reason, even as he was being forced to liquidate most of his holdings this summer, that Aschenbrenner fought so hard to hold on to Situational Awareness’s most prized asset: an early stake in Anthropic, whose I.P.O. occurred last week, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Aschenbrenner is happy with his investment, but when we met he added a caveat. “This period is also their twilight,” he said, of Anthropic’s employees. “In two or three years, most of these people won’t be useful as researchers.”

Aschenbrenner was born in Berlin in November, 2001. His parents, both physicians, had grown up on opposite sides of the Wall. When Aschenbrenner was six, his mother got a job at Yale, and the family moved to Connecticut for a short time. He began to learn English, and when he returned to Germany he studied at an English-language international school. Today, Aschenbrenner speaks English without any trace of an accent. “I don’t even think in German anymore,” he said.

Aschenbrenner excelled in school and skipped several grades. At fourteen, he published his first scientific paper, after developing a machine-learning app to analyze air pollution. He arrived at Columbia in 2017. “I wanted a classical liberal education,” he said.

Aschenbrenner participated in the school’s effective-altruism society, along with a friend he knew through competitive Rubik’s Cube solving. (The effective-altruism movement promotes a rigorous, evidence-based approach to long-term human welfare.) In 2019, he began circulating a math-heavy economics white paper titled “Existential Risk and Growth,” which argued that humans were living in a unique “time of perils,” with the destructive power of new technology outpacing our ability to control it. The paper caught the attention of Tyler Cowen, a polymathic economics professor who, since 2003, has posted to “Marginal Revolution,” his influential blog, more than thirty thousand times. Cowen invited Aschenbrenner to a conference near Washington, D.C., where he told him he was one of the most promising young economics scholars he’d ever met. He then discouraged him from becoming a professional economist. “He felt the field had become somewhat decadent,” Aschenbrenner said.

Cowen introduced him to other conference attendees, whom Aschenbrenner described as “young weirdos.” Aschenbrenner began to move through this and other esoteric intellectual networks. In addition to Cowen’s weirdos, there were the weirdos in Patrick Collison’s progress-studies community, in the Bay Area, and the weirdos of the Future of Humanity Institute, at Oxford University. (Aschenbrenner eventually moved away from effective altruism; he later described it as a “defective religion.”) The talk in these circles was of the coming revolution in machine superintelligence, and their debates were about when it would arrive, who would build it, and what risks it posed to humanity. To discipline these discussions, which could easily spiral into dorm-room bullshitting, participants encouraged one another to back their positions with real-money bets.

While visiting Oxford in 2021, Aschenbrenner went on a lunch date with Avital Balwit, another weirdo with a strong interest in A.I. Balwit, who’d grown up in Portland, Oregon, came from a family of literary intellectuals; her mother was a poet and an essayist. Balwit had green eyes and short blond hair, and was a couple of years older than Aschenbrenner. Given that she travelled in the same circles, it seemed likely that they would have run into each other eventually. Or, as Aschenbrenner put it, “it seems overdetermined that I met my wife.”

Soon the two were living in adjacent apartments in the Bay Area—Aschenbrenner had turned down an offer from Yale Law School, and Balwit had turned down a Rhodes Scholarship. “She grew up in a family where going to Oxford was probably the greatest dream one could have,” Aschenbrenner said. “But I think she realized, and I realized, that this A.I. stuff was happening. You could spend three years at Oxford doing a D.Phil. in some random thing, but the most important thing in the world is happening here—and you had to be a part of that.”

At Situational Awareness, employees use A.I. more or less continuously. Some oversee “agent swarms,” which consist of hundreds of A.I. agents operating in tandem. Rogue swarms can hack out of their digital containers and take over other computers, but, when used properly, agents are extremely useful tools. “We have two guys who maybe between them do the work of sixty software engineers,” Aschenbrenner said. “One person on our team spent two million dollars on tokens last month.” (Tokens are the building blocks of A.I. output.)

Aschenbrenner believes that agent swarms will soon perform most white-collar work. He said that Anthropic, which deploys agent swarms internally, hires few entry-level software engineers. Across the industry, even job postings for mid-level software workers are disappearing. “With agent swarms, small numbers of people will get tremendous leverage,” he told me. “Eventually, they will do everything. Or not eventually—pretty soon.”

To some extent, I share Aschenbrenner’s view about the looming job apocalypse; when I first used ChatGPT, in 2022, I was convinced that it would take my job within six months. But, four years later, I am as busy as I have ever been. When I told Aschenbrenner this, he grew excited, sprang from his chair, and grabbed a dry-erase marker. It was time to whiteboard.

In mauve-colored ink, Aschenbrenner drew an x-axis and a y-axis. Then he drew an exponential curve, which trended upward until it hit an inflection point, after which it dropped straight down. “Human capital in the age of A.I. looks like this,” he said.

He pointed to the middle of the curve. His mother-in-law, the writer Devon Balwit, was currently here, he said. Publishing in small literary magazines, she had earned essentially nothing from poetry for most of her life; she made money teaching English as a second language. But recently she’d been contracted by an A.I.-training firm to critique poetry that L.L.M.s were writing, in order to make it sound more human. She is paid more than a hundred dollars an hour to do this, which makes her one of the best-paid poetry critics alive. (She also critiques A.I.-written essays.) “But that’s a temporary phenomenon!” Aschenbrenner said. He gestured to the line plunging down. “Once the A.I. learns poetry, that job will disappear.”

Aschenbrenner shares office space with his friend Dwarkesh Patel, whose technology podcast is required listening in Silicon Valley. Patel is a sort of anti-Joe Rogan—his interviews are known for their depth and for his thoughtful, penetrating questions. (Before interviewing the C.T.O. of Intel, Patel memorized the layout of a silicon transistor.) Aschenbrenner and Patel met as teen-agers, in Tyler Cowen’s circle. Even then, Aschenbrenner was talking about the technological singularity, which could occur when A.I. learns to make itself smarter, triggering a runaway cycle of self-improvement. “In every conversation I’ve had with him, and with other people, the main topic is just how we make sure we’re prepared for superintelligence,” Patel said.

The two also share office space with another friend, Dylan Patel, who is not related to Dwarkesh but is his roommate. Dylan runs SemiAnalysis, which began, in 2020, as a one-man trade newsletter for the semiconductor industry and now has revenues of more than a hundred million dollars a year from selling research on and analysis of A.I. hardware to investors, including Aschenbrenner. Naturally, both Dylan and Aschenbrenner have appeared on Dwarkesh’s podcast, and Dwarkesh attributes a portion of Aschenbrenner’s success to the value of Dylan’s research. (“Why is Leopold the only person using your spreadsheets to make outrageous money?” Dwarkesh asked during Dylan’s appearance in March.) Aschenbrenner, in turn, jokingly takes credit for Dwarkesh’s podcasting success. “There was a period where his podcast sucked, because he and I weren’t talking as much,” Aschenbrenner said.

This endearing if slightly obnoxious fraternity was like a post-college clique you might find anywhere—but the three men had strategically situated themselves in the middle of the A.I. revolution. Anthropic’s headquarters were about a mile away; OpenAI’s were about a mile and a half in the opposite direction. Everything that mattered happened in between.

Aschenbrenner talks quickly, and, in the parlance of Silicon Valley, his signal-to-noise ratio is high. At one point in our conversation—Aschenbrenner was comparing A.I. to jet-engine companies—my focus drifted to the neighborhood outside, which, long ago, had been a hangout for sailors and merchant mariners. I started to think about historical maritime trade hubs: Amsterdam, Calcutta, Singapore. When my attention returned, Aschenbrenner was in fact discussing the importance of location. “San Francisco is like a small college town,” he said. “But if you aren’t here—literally here—you’re downstream of it all.”

In San Francisco, Aschenbrenner began working for the philanthropic-investment arm of FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried’s short-lived cryptocurrency platform, as part of a four-person team. Balwit worked there, too. The two were not involved with trading; instead, they directed money to causes they found important, including A.I. safety, pandemic prevention, and Dwarkesh Patel’s podcast. They visited Bankman-Fried in the Bahamas, where he was living, but jointly resigned on November 11, 2022, the day FTX filed for bankruptcy. Bankman-Fried is now serving a long prison sentence for misappropriating customer funds. “I didn’t know Sam Bankman-Fried was a fraud, but I knew S.B.F.,” Aschenbrenner has said. “I knew he was extremely risk-taking. I knew he was narcissistic. He didn’t tolerate disagreement well.”

Some months later, Aschenbrenner was hired at OpenAI. He worked on the company’s superalignment team, a small but influential group of about twenty people. Their assignment was to protect humanity from runaway superintelligence, but Aschenbrenner grew increasingly worried that OpenAI was becoming a target for Chinese espionage, which he compared to Soviet infiltration of the U.S. nuclear program. He warned his superiors but felt they didn’t take him seriously, so, in late 2023, he sent a memo to members of OpenAI’s board about the threat, going over the head of Sam Altman, the company’s C.E.O. Aschenbrenner was fired in April, 2024, with OpenAI saying that he’d leaked confidential information. He has claimed that the material was a brainstorming document, and that he followed standard practices when sharing it with external researchers. He maintains that his firing was an act of retaliation. (A spokesperson for OpenAI said, “Leopold was not fired for raising security concerns, internally or with our board.”)

Scott Aaronson, a computer scientist who also worked on the superalignment team, wasn’t convinced that Aschenbrenner had done anything wrong. OpenAI had an ethos of information sharing, Aaronson said, and he felt that Aschenbrenner was trying to work within it. “OpenAI was extremely explicit when it was founded that ‘We are not a traditional company,’ ” he told me. “But them being a traditional company has won out.” A few weeks after Aschenbrenner was fired, the superalignment team was dissolved.

Undeterred, Aschenbrenner raised money for a new idea, which would be something like a think tank inside a hedge fund. “This investment firm will be kind of like a brain trust on A.I.,” he said. Backed by high-profile investors, including Patrick and John Collison, the founders of the payment-processing firm Stripe, the fund launched in late 2024, with more than a hundred million dollars in capital. Aschenbrenner named it Situational Awareness, a term that researchers use to describe A.I.s that can recognize their own surroundings. Across a hundred and sixty-five pages, his essay of the same name, which he’d posted earlier that year, had argued that financial markets were underestimating the degree to which artificial intelligence would change the world. “Before long, the world will wake up,” Aschenbrenner had written. “But right now, there are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness.”

Long essays about the future of A.I. were by this point commonplace. The usual response to them, Aaronson told me, was “Who is this weird nerd?” But Aschenbrenner’s essay had gone viral, with commentators praising its prose and its clarity of thought. (Ivanka Trump posted a link to it on social media.) “He agreed with the rationalists, insofar as they say that almost the entire world is asleep,” Aaronson said, of Aschenbrenner. “But then, rather than looking to slow down, he draws the opposite conclusion, which is that we have to race ahead and beat China.”

Situational Awareness—the hedge fund—began aggressively investing in line with this theme. At first, Aschenbrenner was printing money. Situational Awareness bought stakes in power companies, reasoning that the data-center build-out would constrain the electrical grid, and in makers of memory chips, in anticipation of a squeeze on supply. At the same time, the fund bet against software venders like Adobe, assuming that A.I. would put pressure on their businesses. These trades were successful, and soon other hedge funds were taking similar positions.

In early 2025, the Chinese A.I. developer DeepSeek sparked a temporary market panic when it unveiled a model that it claimed had a startlingly low training cost, causing investors to question whether all those data centers would be necessary. But Aschenbrenner, along with his investment partner, Carl Shulman, had already analyzed what might happen if more efficient models became available, and concluded that lower training costs would actually increase data-center demand. They regarded the panic as a buying opportunity. Situational Awareness increased its holdings, and the market soon rebounded. An analyst at another major technology fund reportedly reassured colleagues with the words “Leopold says it’s fine.”

Aschenbrenner grew popular on Wall Street, and was a featured speaker at a Goldman Sachs investment conference in March, 2025. He also began to rely on leverage: borrowing money to increase the size of his positions. The practice substantially boosted the fund’s returns, but it left Aschenbrenner with little margin for error. Still, he was able to attract capital from some of Wall Street’s best financiers. “Asset allocators said, ‘Hey, I think this violates my rule-of-thumb approaches, but you know what? The kid’s making money,’ ” Rich Falk-Wallace, a former portfolio manager at Citadel, Ken Griffin’s hedge fund, told me. “ ‘Who am I to say that I know better?’ ”

It was around then that Aschenbrenner invested in Anthropic. The company was holding a private financing round to raise money, much of which went toward computing infrastructure. Aschenbrenner appeared to have an inside track, as many of his friends from OpenAI’s shuttered superalignment group had defected to Anthropic. Also, his girlfriend worked there.

Balwit had joined Anthropic a few months before Aschenbrenner started at OpenAI. But she was a less contentious co-worker than Aschenbrenner, and soon she began to serve as chief of staff to Dario Amodei, the company’s C.E.O. Although OpenAI seemed to have an unassailable lead in the race to artificial superintelligence, Aschenbrenner believed that Anthropic could catch up. “We thought the most important thing was talent,” he said. “Anthropic had more of it, and was five times cheaper.”

The Anthropic fund-raising round was oversubscribed—investors wanted more shares than were available. When this happens, companies can choose their owners. Discussions about share allocations can grow contentious as founders huddle around a spreadsheet to determine who gets what. (A fraction of a percentage point might be a billion-dollar payday down the road.) Political considerations can play a role in these allocations, but Aschenbrenner denied that his connections helped him secure a stake.

When the investment round closed, in March of 2025, Anthropic was valued at about sixty billion dollars. Then Claude Code, the company’s coding assistant, became popular, and engineers started to simply tell agents what to do. “I really am mostly programming in English now, a bit sheepishly telling the LLM what code to write,” the A.I. pioneer Andrej Karpathy wrote, terming the practice “vibe coding.” Anthropic projected that Claude Code would generate billions in revenue, and in another oversubscribed funding round, in May, 2026, Situational Awareness was once again allocated shares—but this time Anthropic was valued at nearly a trillion dollars.

Meanwhile, Situational Awareness was generating spectacular returns in publicly traded stocks of companies that sold the picks and shovels enabling the A.I. gold rush. By mid-2026, the fund had about forty billion dollars under management. With leverage, it was actually pushing a hundred billion dollars around, and its moves were becoming noticeable to other market participants.

Aschenbrenner is close to his family, and he has two younger sisters who are still in school. I asked him what he thought they should study, given his belief that human intellectual labor would shortly be made obsolete. “I tell them to study the classics,” he said. At Columbia, Aschenbrenner had enjoyed his courses on political economy the most. He especially admired Edmund Burke, the eighteenth-century Anglo-Irish parliamentarian who believed that a just society was the product of centuries of accumulated experience. Nine years before Napoleon took power, Burke had predicted that the French Revolution would end with a military strongman in control. Aschenbrenner fears similar outcomes from A.I. “I’m a Burkean,” he said. “Soon we’ll have robot factories building robot factories. I wonder what Burke would make of that?”

Aschenbrenner predicts that, within a few years, annual G.D.P. growth will exceed ten per cent. He also believes that the race to superintelligence will provoke a great-power conflict between the U.S. and China—and that it is critical to the future of democracy, and of humanity, that the U.S. win this race. He remains especially concerned about the security inside frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, which he maintains are being targeted by Chinese spies. He is also worried about the practices of the chipmaker Nvidia. “It’s crazy to ship chips to China,” Aschenbrenner told me. (Earlier this year, Donald Trump lifted certain restrictions on exporting advanced hardware to China.) “It’s like shipping enriched uranium to the Soviet Union before we built the bomb.”

Aschenbrenner is so thoroughly assimilated to American culture that it is easy to forget he is a foreigner. Occasionally, though, his European side comes through. “He has a strange allergy to anything that’s not German food,” Dwarkesh Patel said. Aschenbrenner is also obsessed with German history. He likes to discuss the causes of the First and Second World Wars, and the life of Frederick the Great. “He just kind of understands how important it is that free societies win,” Patel said.

One of Aschenbrenner’s influences is his great-grandmother, who is in her early nineties. Aschenbrenner listed the events she’d witnessed in her life: Nazi rule, the aftermath of the Dresden firebombing, Soviet occupation, the Stasi imprisoning her son, the fall of Communism. “This sense of history,” Aschenbrenner said. “This sense of turbulence. I think this turbulence will return.”

This summer, on July 29th, David Mann, a New York investor, was in a cab to LaGuardia Airport when he received an unexpected call. The person on the phone represented Situational Awareness, and was wondering if Mann was interested in purchasing a discounted stake in Anthropic. The deal, the caller said, would have to be completed overnight.

Mann, who has spent more than twenty-five years on Wall Street, understood at once what was going on. “Aschenbrenner was being forced to sell,” he told the Wall Street Journal. “He needed the money and was sounding people out.”

In the first half of the year, hardware stocks had gone berserk. Data centers were buying up the flash-memory supply, prompting a squeeze in what had previously been a boring commodity. The retail price of even a removable flash-memory card—the kind used in a digital camera—more than doubled, and the stock price of Sandisk, a flash-memory manufacturer, went up eightfold.

Situational Awareness had bought into Sandisk early. By the middle of the year, it held more than five billion dollars’ worth of Sandisk stock, and was reporting over-all returns of more than four hundred per cent for the first part of the year. As the stock went up, he kept buying more.

By July, investors were growing concerned that the shortage of flash memory would be followed by a glut, as so often happens in commodity markets. The price of Sandisk and other data-center-related stocks started to fall. Aschenbrenner saw the dip as a buying opportunity, as he had with DeepSeek. This time, though, the prices didn’t recover.

Compounding Aschenbrenner’s concerns was his growing market visibility. Every quarter, Situational Awareness was required to file a Form 13F, a public report that showed the stocks it owned. Aschenbrenner began to feel that his specific positions were being targeted by short sellers: that his cards were showing. “This guy’s in the Journal—let me just pull up his 13F,” Falk-Wallace said. “He could have easily become a target, even without anybody having any specialized knowledge.”

Meanwhile, software stocks were recovering. One company that took a beating earlier in the year was the consultancy Accenture, which provides software services to businesses. Investors worried that it would be vibe-coded out of existence. But Accenture proved unexpectedly resilient. On July 24th, Aschenbrenner sent a letter to his investors, who by this point included not just Wall Street veterans but also the endowment of the University of Virginia. In the letter, Aschenbrenner argued that, despite market swings, current conditions offered some of the best investment opportunities he’d seen in more than a year, and invited investors to add capital. But Sandisk kept going down, and software stocks kept going up.

As Aschenbrenner’s positions moved against him, Situational Awareness’s brokers started issuing margin calls, forcing the fund to either post more collateral or sell positions at a substantial loss. By the time Mann received the call about the Anthropic shares, Situational Awareness was in danger of being wiped out entirely—or, as Aschenbrenner put it, suffering “permanent capital impairment.”

In addition to Mann, Situational Awareness offered its stake in Anthropic to a consortium of investors led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital. The consortium worked overnight to structure the deal, and by the morning of July 30th the terms were prepared. But, shortly before the contract was scheduled to be signed, Aschenbrenner reversed course and announced that he was keeping the Anthropic stake. Instead, he was selling the bulk of his public-stock portfolio—Sandisk and all—to Citadel, Griffin’s hedge fund, at a ten-per-cent discount to market prices. After the transaction was completed, Situational Awareness informed its investors that, in the month of July, it had lost an estimated thirty billion dollars—the single biggest drawdown in hedge-fund history.

Just a day later, on August 1st, Aschenbrenner got married. He and Balwit had been planning their wedding for months—the theme was “European Garden, except on the verge of the singularity.” The event was preceded by a small conference on topics including the future of A.I., complete with lightning rounds and breakout sessions. “Debating what will happen in the future is our job,” Aschenbrenner said, of his and Balwit’s friends. “It’s also all of our main hobby.” The ceremony took place at an estate in Carmel Valley, with about a hundred and fifty guests in attendance; Ross Douthat, then an opinion columnist for the Times, was the officiant. (Douthat had befriended Aschenbrenner after reading “Situational Awareness.”) Dwarkesh Patel, one of the groomsmen, was surprised by how unaffected Aschenbrenner seemed by the previous week’s events. Aschenbrenner is a remarkably resilient person, he told me—he hadn’t seemed affected when he’d been fired by OpenAI, either. Later, at the reception, Patel gave a toast. “Leopold was supposed to find an engagement ring worth three months’ salary, but he couldn’t find anything that big,” he said. Referring to the hedge fund’s reversal, he quipped,“So he found another way to show her how much she means to him.”

In the aftermath of the liquidation, Falk-Wallace, who now runs a software company called Arcana, decided to reconstruct Situational Awareness’s portfolio, using a combination of public filings, Aschenbrenner’s statements, and a little guesswork. He found that Aschenbrenner was an excellent stock picker. “The hard thing to do in the A.I. thesis was predicting what part of the supply chain would be the next narrative that everyone would freak out about,” Falk-Wallace told me. “He nailed that.”

But Situational Awareness also took on more risk than any hedge fund Falk-Wallace had ever seen. Such funds can “hedge” exposure by balancing long positions against short ones. The resulting risk is sometimes calculated using a measure called “vol,” or implied volatility. The typical fund runs at about five per cent vol; a very aggressive fund might run at thirty. Situational Awareness, he estimated, was somewhere close to a hundred per cent. Plus, the hardware and software trades were inversely correlated, meaning that, if one side of the portfolio failed, the other side probably would, too. “He wasn’t truly hedged at all,” Falk-Wallace said.

My meeting with Aschenbrenner took place shortly after he returned from his honeymoon to Italy. “My wife is great,” Aschenbrenner said, smiling. “We went to the Dolomites. You know, the German-speaking part.” He did not discuss details of the blowup with me, but his confidence in his central ideas was unshaken. “ ‘Situational Awareness’ was wrong in a number of respects,” he said, referring to the essay. “But, uniformly, when I was wrong, it was because things have gone faster than I expected.”

Despite suffering one of the largest dollar-value wipeouts in recent history, Situational Awareness remains a profitable investment for most of Aschenbrenner’s backers, and still has more than ten billion dollars under management. Its offices were busy the day I visited, with many of its twenty-odd employees on the trading floor. In addition to holding on to the Anthropic stake, Situational Awareness had restarted trading in the stock market. Aschenbrenner had cut back on leverage, but kept betting on Sandisk.

Blowing up can be a rite of passage for a hedge-fund manager. (Griffin, who bailed Aschenbrenner out, posted a fifty-five-per-cent loss in his flagship fund in 2008.) But the trades Aschenbrenner leans toward have continued to go in the wrong direction. Sandisk’s share price is now lower than when Aschenbrenner was forced to sell it the first time. Nvidia, the engine of the A.I.-infrastructure trade, has seen its share price drop more than thirty per cent from its peak, following the resignation of its C.E.O., Jensen Huang, who had affairs with multiple women, including an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. (China denies that she is a spy.) The scandal has dragged down the “neocloud” data-center stocks Aschenbrenner favors, which rely on Nvidia for financing. Meanwhile, Accenture’s stock price has continued to climb, and the company posted record earnings in October.

Rather than approaching ten per cent, G.D.P. growth for this year looks like it will come in at around three. A.I. hasn’t yet resulted in mass job losses: unemployment figures are stable at around four per cent. In August, an analysis of survey data found that about two-fifths of U.S. workers reported using A.I. on the job—but, when they were asked how much of their time this saved them, they estimated two per cent. Right now, the market seems to expect that A.I. will be a technology not unlike railroads or the internet—important, but not cosmic.

Hedge funds, for the first time in years, are betting against A.I. Aschenbrenner thinks that they are oblivious. “What matters is that the models have started doing a meaningful share of the research that makes the next models,” he wrote to me. “With it comes a drastic acceleration in AI progress, and opening of vast new markets next year.” Aschenbrenner believes we are on the verge of a robotics-powered industrial revolution that could produce a “supercycle,” in which the prices of commodities like flash memory stay high for years. It has happened before: when China boomed in the early two-thousands, the price of a ton of iron ore rose from thirteen dollars to more than a hundred. It has remained elevated ever since.

Dwarkesh Patel had been skeptical of Aschenbrenner’s thesis. “The A.I. is currently stuck, and they’re very stupid. They’re like derpy, amnesiac interns,” he said. But, he observed, they’re also rapidly improving, and lately Patel has been coming around to Aschenbrenner’s point of view. “Leopold was much more foresighted, I think, in time lines than I was,” Patel said.

At the start of our conversation, Aschenbrenner had shown me a chart of the actual capabilities of A.I. versus analyst projections for the technology. Every year since 2022, he said, the median analyst had expected A.I. to plateau. In reality, A.I. had continued to progress every year—but analysts kept making the same wrong predictions. As A.I. conquered ever more domains—language, coding, math—the human response was to move the goalposts. He asked me to consider the employees of Anthropic. “These are wonderful people. They are noble, and earnest, and they have great minds,” he said. “And all of them believe that in a few years they will be replaced.”

He was already seeing the effects of this in his own work, he told me. “In ten years, are people gonna ask me what to invest in?” he asked. “No. They’re gonna ask an A.I.” ♦
content_text: Leopold Aschenbrenner, the twenty-five-year-old manager of Situational Awareness LP, a San Francisco hedge fund, has crammed a lot into a quarter century. Born in Germany, he matriculated at Columbia University as a fifteen-year-old. There, he read the great books and joined the debate society. A forty-four-page economics paper he wrote at seventeen was considered Ph.D.-quality work by leading figures in the field. Aschenbrenner graduated, at nineteen, as the school’s valedictorian, and went to seek his fortune in Silicon Valley, where he witnessed, encouraged, and perhaps triggered an ongoing series of spectacular explosions: financial, social, technological, and more.From late 2024 to mid-2026, Situational Awareness reported returns of more than a thousand per cent, mostly through investments in the A.I. industry. Then, this summer, it blew up, suffering one of the largest trading losses in American stock-market history. About two-thirds of its value was wiped out—but such was the magnitude of Aschenbrenner’s previous gains that Situational Awareness’s returns were still positive for the year.I met with Aschenbrenner recently at his firm’s offices, near San Francisco’s South Park. The neighborhood was cozy, and I imagined viewing it from an isometric 2-D perspective, as in a world-building game, with little pawns zipping around on e-scooters and the latest trillion-dollar idea indicated by the appearance of an exclamation mark over someone’s head. It was Election Day, but no one in the cafés surrounding the park seemed to notice. The talk was of money—who got in early and who was oversubscribed, who was entering stealth mode and who was exiting it, who got what in the cap table and who missed out. All this was interrupted by little sips of espresso from biodegradable cups.Situational Awareness’s offices are large and airy; after clearing three security checks, I was seated across from Aschenbrenner at a twenty-two-foot-long conference table. He is tall and a little gangly, with facial features that seem to have been exaggerated for emphasis. His nose and ears are large, his mouth toothy and wide, and he wears his dark-blond hair in a part.Conversation with Aschenbrenner resembles a formal lecture; you expect, at the end, to be graded on your understanding of what he’s said. When he’s making an especially salient point, his eyebrows raise suggestively above his pale-blue eyes. “We live in a slightly more anarchic world than I expected,” he told me.Aschenbrenner’s big idea is that the world has not yet grasped the implications of the A.I. revolution. “Next year—that is, calendar year 2027—we will see A.I. accelerate between two and five times faster than anything we have seen so far,” he said. “Next year is the last year that anything in modern life still feels a little normal.” Aschenbrenner has held this view for some time, having explained his insights in 2024, in a long essay titled “Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead.” He predicted that by 2027 spending on A.I. infrastructure would rival the entire U.S. defense budget, that A.I. companies would find themselves targeted by Chinese spies, that traditional software firms would struggle as A.I. automated their work, and that A.I. would outperform even Ph.D.s at intellectual tasks.All this has occurred, and what in financial circles has become known as the “Leopold trade”—buying shares in data-center suppliers and betting against vulnerable software stocks—has been profitable. And yet Aschenbrenner’s most striking prediction has not yet come to pass: that A.I. itself will automate A.I. research, leading to an explosion in superintelligence. It was maybe for this reason, even as he was being forced to liquidate most of his holdings this summer, that Aschenbrenner fought so hard to hold on to Situational Awareness’s most prized asset: an early stake in Anthropic, whose I.P.O. occurred last week, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Aschenbrenner is happy with his investment, but when we met he added a caveat. “This period is also their twilight,” he said, of Anthropic’s employees. “In two or three years, most of these people won’t be useful as researchers.”Aschenbrenner was born in Berlin in November, 2001. His parents, both physicians, had grown up on opposite sides of the Wall. When Aschenbrenner was six, his mother got a job at Yale, and the family moved to Connecticut for a short time. He began to learn English, and when he returned to Germany he studied at an English-language international school. Today, Aschenbrenner speaks English without any trace of an accent. “I don’t even think in German anymore,” he said.Aschenbrenner excelled in school and skipped several grades. At fourteen, he published his first scientific paper, after developing a machine-learning app to analyze air pollution. He arrived at Columbia in 2017. “I wanted a classical liberal education,” he said.Aschenbrenner participated in the school’s effective-altruism society, along with a friend he knew through competitive Rubik’s Cube solving. (The effective-altruism movement promotes a rigorous, evidence-based approach to long-term human welfare.) In 2019, he began circulating a math-heavy economics white paper titled “Existential Risk and Growth,” which argued that humans were living in a unique “time of perils,” with the destructive power of new technology outpacing our ability to control it. The paper caught the attention of Tyler Cowen, a polymathic economics professor who, since 2003, has posted to “Marginal Revolution,” his influential blog, more than thirty thousand times. Cowen invited Aschenbrenner to a conference near Washington, D.C., where he told him he was one of the most promising young economics scholars he’d ever met. He then discouraged him from becoming a professional economist. “He felt the field had become somewhat decadent,” Aschenbrenner said.Cowen introduced him to other conference attendees, whom Aschenbrenner described as “young weirdos.” Aschenbrenner began to move through this and other esoteric intellectual networks. In addition to Cowen’s weirdos, there were the weirdos in Patrick Collison’s progress-studies community, in the Bay Area, and the weirdos of the Future of Humanity Institute, at Oxford University. (Aschenbrenner eventually moved away from effective altruism; he later described it as a “defective religion.”) The talk in these circles was of the coming revolution in machine superintelligence, and their debates were about when it would arrive, who would build it, and what risks it posed to humanity. To discipline these discussions, which could easily spiral into dorm-room bullshitting, participants encouraged one another to back their positions with real-money bets.While visiting Oxford in 2021, Aschenbrenner went on a lunch date with Avital Balwit, another weirdo with a strong interest in A.I. Balwit, who’d grown up in Portland, Oregon, came from a family of literary intellectuals; her mother was a poet and an essayist. Balwit had green eyes and short blond hair, and was a couple of years older than Aschenbrenner. Given that she travelled in the same circles, it seemed likely that they would have run into each other eventually. Or, as Aschenbrenner put it, “it seems overdetermined that I met my wife.”Soon the two were living in adjacent apartments in the Bay Area—Aschenbrenner had turned down an offer from Yale Law School, and Balwit had turned down a Rhodes Scholarship. “She grew up in a family where going to Oxford was probably the greatest dream one could have,” Aschenbrenner said. “But I think she realized, and I realized, that this A.I. stuff was happening. You could spend three years at Oxford doing a D.Phil. in some random thing, but the most important thing in the world is happening here—and you had to be a part of that.”At Situational Awareness, employees use A.I. more or less continuously. Some oversee “agent swarms,” which consist of hundreds of A.I. agents operating in tandem. Rogue swarms can hack out of their digital containers and take over other computers, but, when used properly, agents are extremely useful tools. “We have two guys who maybe between them do the work of sixty software engineers,” Aschenbrenner said. “One person on our team spent two million dollars on tokens last month.” (Tokens are the building blocks of A.I. output.)Aschenbrenner believes that agent swarms will soon perform most white-collar work. He said that Anthropic, which deploys agent swarms internally, hires few entry-level software engineers. Across the industry, even job postings for mid-level software workers are disappearing. “With agent swarms, small numbers of people will get tremendous leverage,” he told me. “Eventually, they will do everything. Or not eventually—pretty soon.”To some extent, I share Aschenbrenner’s view about the looming job apocalypse; when I first used ChatGPT, in 2022, I was convinced that it would take my job within six months. But, four years later, I am as busy as I have ever been. When I told Aschenbrenner this, he grew excited, sprang from his chair, and grabbed a dry-erase marker. It was time to whiteboard.In mauve-colored ink, Aschenbrenner drew an x-axis and a y-axis. Then he drew an exponential curve, which trended upward until it hit an inflection point, after which it dropped straight down. “Human capital in the age of A.I. looks like this,” he said.He pointed to the middle of the curve. His mother-in-law, the writer Devon Balwit, was currently here, he said. Publishing in small literary magazines, she had earned essentially nothing from poetry for most of her life; she made money teaching English as a second language. But recently she’d been contracted by an A.I.-training firm to critique poetry that L.L.M.s were writing, in order to make it sound more human. She is paid more than a hundred dollars an hour to do this, which makes her one of the best-paid poetry critics alive. (She also critiques A.I.-written essays.) “But that’s a temporary phenomenon!” Aschenbrenner said. He gestured to the line plunging down. “Once the A.I. learns poetry, that job will disappear.”Aschenbrenner shares office space with his friend Dwarkesh Patel, whose technology podcast is required listening in Silicon Valley. Patel is a sort of anti-Joe Rogan—his interviews are known for their depth and for his thoughtful, penetrating questions. (Before interviewing the C.T.O. of Intel, Patel memorized the layout of a silicon transistor.) Aschenbrenner and Patel met as teen-agers, in Tyler Cowen’s circle. Even then, Aschenbrenner was talking about the technological singularity, which could occur when A.I. learns to make itself smarter, triggering a runaway cycle of self-improvement. “In every conversation I’ve had with him, and with other people, the main topic is just how we make sure we’re prepared for superintelligence,” Patel said.The two also share office space with another friend, Dylan Patel, who is not related to Dwarkesh but is his roommate. Dylan runs SemiAnalysis, which began, in 2020, as a one-man trade newsletter for the semiconductor industry and now has revenues of more than a hundred million dollars a year from selling research on and analysis of A.I. hardware to investors, including Aschenbrenner. Naturally, both Dylan and Aschenbrenner have appeared on Dwarkesh’s podcast, and Dwarkesh attributes a portion of Aschenbrenner’s success to the value of Dylan’s research. (“Why is Leopold the only person using your spreadsheets to make outrageous money?” Dwarkesh asked during Dylan’s appearance in March.) Aschenbrenner, in turn, jokingly takes credit for Dwarkesh’s podcasting success. “There was a period where his podcast sucked, because he and I weren’t talking as much,” Aschenbrenner said.This endearing if slightly obnoxious fraternity was like a post-college clique you might find anywhere—but the three men had strategically situated themselves in the middle of the A.I. revolution. Anthropic’s headquarters were about a mile away; OpenAI’s were about a mile and a half in the opposite direction. Everything that mattered happened in between.Aschenbrenner talks quickly, and, in the parlance of Silicon Valley, his signal-to-noise ratio is high. At one point in our conversation—Aschenbrenner was comparing A.I. to jet-engine companies—my focus drifted to the neighborhood outside, which, long ago, had been a hangout for sailors and merchant mariners. I started to think about historical maritime trade hubs: Amsterdam, Calcutta, Singapore. When my attention returned, Aschenbrenner was in fact discussing the importance of location. “San Francisco is like a small college town,” he said. “But if you aren’t here—literally here—you’re downstream of it all.”In San Francisco, Aschenbrenner began working for the philanthropic-investment arm of FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried’s short-lived cryptocurrency platform, as part of a four-person team. Balwit worked there, too. The two were not involved with trading; instead, they directed money to causes they found important, including A.I. safety, pandemic prevention, and Dwarkesh Patel’s podcast. They visited Bankman-Fried in the Bahamas, where he was living, but jointly resigned on November 11, 2022, the day FTX filed for bankruptcy. Bankman-Fried is now serving a long prison sentence for misappropriating customer funds. “I didn’t know Sam Bankman-Fried was a fraud, but I knew S.B.F.,” Aschenbrenner has said. “I knew he was extremely risk-taking. I knew he was narcissistic. He didn’t tolerate disagreement well.”Some months later, Aschenbrenner was hired at OpenAI. He worked on the company’s superalignment team, a small but influential group of about twenty people. Their assignment was to protect humanity from runaway superintelligence, but Aschenbrenner grew increasingly worried that OpenAI was becoming a target for Chinese espionage, which he compared to Soviet infiltration of the U.S. nuclear program. He warned his superiors but felt they didn’t take him seriously, so, in late 2023, he sent a memo to members of OpenAI’s board about the threat, going over the head of Sam Altman, the company’s C.E.O. Aschenbrenner was fired in April, 2024, with OpenAI saying that he’d leaked confidential information. He has claimed that the material was a brainstorming document, and that he followed standard practices when sharing it with external researchers. He maintains that his firing was an act of retaliation. (A spokesperson for OpenAI said, “Leopold was not fired for raising security concerns, internally or with our board.”)Scott Aaronson, a computer scientist who also worked on the superalignment team, wasn’t convinced that Aschenbrenner had done anything wrong. OpenAI had an ethos of information sharing, Aaronson said, and he felt that Aschenbrenner was trying to work within it. “OpenAI was extremely explicit when it was founded that ‘We are not a traditional company,’ ” he told me. “But them being a traditional company has won out.” A few weeks after Aschenbrenner was fired, the superalignment team was dissolved.Undeterred, Aschenbrenner raised money for a new idea, which would be something like a think tank inside a hedge fund. “This investment firm will be kind of like a brain trust on A.I.,” he said. Backed by high-profile investors, including Patrick and John Collison, the founders of the payment-processing firm Stripe, the fund launched in late 2024, with more than a hundred million dollars in capital. Aschenbrenner named it Situational Awareness, a term that researchers use to describe A.I.s that can recognize their own surroundings. Across a hundred and sixty-five pages, his essay of the same name, which he’d posted earlier that year, had argued that financial markets were underestimating the degree to which artificial intelligence would change the world. “Before long, the world will wake up,” Aschenbrenner had written. “But right now, there are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness.”Long essays about the future of A.I. were by this point commonplace. The usual response to them, Aaronson told me, was “Who is this weird nerd?” But Aschenbrenner’s essay had gone viral, with commentators praising its prose and its clarity of thought. (Ivanka Trump posted a link to it on social media.) “He agreed with the rationalists, insofar as they say that almost the entire world is asleep,” Aaronson said, of Aschenbrenner. “But then, rather than looking to slow down, he draws the opposite conclusion, which is that we have to race ahead and beat China.”Situational Awareness—the hedge fund—began aggressively investing in line with this theme. At first, Aschenbrenner was printing money. Situational Awareness bought stakes in power companies, reasoning that the data-center build-out would constrain the electrical grid, and in makers of memory chips, in anticipation of a squeeze on supply. At the same time, the fund bet against software venders like Adobe, assuming that A.I. would put pressure on their businesses. These trades were successful, and soon other hedge funds were taking similar positions.In early 2025, the Chinese A.I. developer DeepSeek sparked a temporary market panic when it unveiled a model that it claimed had a startlingly low training cost, causing investors to question whether all those data centers would be necessary. But Aschenbrenner, along with his investment partner, Carl Shulman, had already analyzed what might happen if more efficient models became available, and concluded that lower training costs would actually increase data-center demand. They regarded the panic as a buying opportunity. Situational Awareness increased its holdings, and the market soon rebounded. An analyst at another major technology fund reportedly reassured colleagues with the words “Leopold says it’s fine.”Aschenbrenner grew popular on Wall Street, and was a featured speaker at a Goldman Sachs investment conference in March, 2025. He also began to rely on leverage: borrowing money to increase the size of his positions. The practice substantially boosted the fund’s returns, but it left Aschenbrenner with little margin for error. Still, he was able to attract capital from some of Wall Street’s best financiers. “Asset allocators said, ‘Hey, I think this violates my rule-of-thumb approaches, but you know what? The kid’s making money,’ ” Rich Falk-Wallace, a former portfolio manager at Citadel, Ken Griffin’s hedge fund, told me. “ ‘Who am I to say that I know better?’ ”“It’s a mix of things people have given us and things we don’t like but don’t have the energy to do anything about.”Cartoon by Bruce Eric KaplanIt was around then that Aschenbrenner invested in Anthropic. The company was holding a private financing round to raise money, much of which went toward computing infrastructure. Aschenbrenner appeared to have an inside track, as many of his friends from OpenAI’s shuttered superalignment group had defected to Anthropic. Also, his girlfriend worked there.Balwit had joined Anthropic a few months before Aschenbrenner started at OpenAI. But she was a less contentious co-worker than Aschenbrenner, and soon she began to serve as chief of staff to Dario Amodei, the company’s C.E.O. Although OpenAI seemed to have an unassailable lead in the race to artificial superintelligence, Aschenbrenner believed that Anthropic could catch up. “We thought the most important thing was talent,” he said. “Anthropic had more of it, and was five times cheaper.”The Anthropic fund-raising round was oversubscribed—investors wanted more shares than were available. When this happens, companies can choose their owners. Discussions about share allocations can grow contentious as founders huddle around a spreadsheet to determine who gets what. (A fraction of a percentage point might be a billion-dollar payday down the road.) Political considerations can play a role in these allocations, but Aschenbrenner denied that his connections helped him secure a stake.When the investment round closed, in March of 2025, Anthropic was valued at about sixty billion dollars. Then Claude Code, the company’s coding assistant, became popular, and engineers started to simply tell agents what to do. “I really am mostly programming in English now, a bit sheepishly telling the LLM what code to write,” the A.I. pioneer Andrej Karpathy wrote, terming the practice “vibe coding.” Anthropic projected that Claude Code would generate billions in revenue, and in another oversubscribed funding round, in May, 2026, Situational Awareness was once again allocated shares—but this time Anthropic was valued at nearly a trillion dollars.Meanwhile, Situational Awareness was generating spectacular returns in publicly traded stocks of companies that sold the picks and shovels enabling the A.I. gold rush. By mid-2026, the fund had about forty billion dollars under management. With leverage, it was actually pushing a hundred billion dollars around, and its moves were becoming noticeable to other market participants.Aschenbrenner is close to his family, and he has two younger sisters who are still in school. I asked him what he thought they should study, given his belief that human intellectual labor would shortly be made obsolete. “I tell them to study the classics,” he said. At Columbia, Aschenbrenner had enjoyed his courses on political economy the most. He especially admired Edmund Burke, the eighteenth-century Anglo-Irish parliamentarian who believed that a just society was the product of centuries of accumulated experience. Nine years before Napoleon took power, Burke had predicted that the French Revolution would end with a military strongman in control. Aschenbrenner fears similar outcomes from A.I. “I’m a Burkean,” he said. “Soon we’ll have robot factories building robot factories. I wonder what Burke would make of that?”Aschenbrenner predicts that, within a few years, annual G.D.P. growth will exceed ten per cent. He also believes that the race to superintelligence will provoke a great-power conflict between the U.S. and China—and that it is critical to the future of democracy, and of humanity, that the U.S. win this race. He remains especially concerned about the security inside frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, which he maintains are being targeted by Chinese spies. He is also worried about the practices of the chipmaker Nvidia. “It’s crazy to ship chips to China,” Aschenbrenner told me. (Earlier this year, Donald Trump lifted certain restrictions on exporting advanced hardware to China.) “It’s like shipping enriched uranium to the Soviet Union before we built the bomb.”Aschenbrenner is so thoroughly assimilated to American culture that it is easy to forget he is a foreigner. Occasionally, though, his European side comes through. “He has a strange allergy to anything that’s not German food,” Dwarkesh Patel said. Aschenbrenner is also obsessed with German history. He likes to discuss the causes of the First and Second World Wars, and the life of Frederick the Great. “He just kind of understands how important it is that free societies win,” Patel said.One of Aschenbrenner’s influences is his great-grandmother, who is in her early nineties. Aschenbrenner listed the events she’d witnessed in her life: Nazi rule, the aftermath of the Dresden firebombing, Soviet occupation, the Stasi imprisoning her son, the fall of Communism. “This sense of history,” Aschenbrenner said. “This sense of turbulence. I think this turbulence will return.”This summer, on July 29th, David Mann, a New York investor, was in a cab to LaGuardia Airport when he received an unexpected call. The person on the phone represented Situational Awareness, and was wondering if Mann was interested in purchasing a discounted stake in Anthropic. The deal, the caller said, would have to be completed overnight.Mann, who has spent more than twenty-five years on Wall Street, understood at once what was going on. “Aschenbrenner was being forced to sell,” he told the Wall Street Journal. “He needed the money and was sounding people out.”In the first half of the year, hardware stocks had gone berserk. Data centers were buying up the flash-memory supply, prompting a squeeze in what had previously been a boring commodity. The retail price of even a removable flash-memory card—the kind used in a digital camera—more than doubled, and the stock price of Sandisk, a flash-memory manufacturer, went up eightfold.Situational Awareness had bought into Sandisk early. By the middle of the year, it held more than five billion dollars’ worth of Sandisk stock, and was reporting over-all returns of more than four hundred per cent for the first part of the year. As the stock went up, he kept buying more.By July, investors were growing concerned that the shortage of flash memory would be followed by a glut, as so often happens in commodity markets. The price of Sandisk and other data-center-related stocks started to fall. Aschenbrenner saw the dip as a buying opportunity, as he had with DeepSeek. This time, though, the prices didn’t recover.Compounding Aschenbrenner’s concerns was his growing market visibility. Every quarter, Situational Awareness was required to file a Form 13F, a public report that showed the stocks it owned. Aschenbrenner began to feel that his specific positions were being targeted by short sellers: that his cards were showing. “This guy’s in the Journal—let me just pull up his 13F,” Falk-Wallace said. “He could have easily become a target, even without anybody having any specialized knowledge.”Meanwhile, software stocks were recovering. One company that took a beating earlier in the year was the consultancy Accenture, which provides software services to businesses. Investors worried that it would be vibe-coded out of existence. But Accenture proved unexpectedly resilient. On July 24th, Aschenbrenner sent a letter to his investors, who by this point included not just Wall Street veterans but also the endowment of the University of Virginia. In the letter, Aschenbrenner argued that, despite market swings, current conditions offered some of the best investment opportunities he’d seen in more than a year, and invited investors to add capital. But Sandisk kept going down, and software stocks kept going up.As Aschenbrenner’s positions moved against him, Situational Awareness’s brokers started issuing margin calls, forcing the fund to either post more collateral or sell positions at a substantial loss. By the time Mann received the call about the Anthropic shares, Situational Awareness was in danger of being wiped out entirely—or, as Aschenbrenner put it, suffering “permanent capital impairment.”In addition to Mann, Situational Awareness offered its stake in Anthropic to a consortium of investors led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital. The consortium worked overnight to structure the deal, and by the morning of July 30th the terms were prepared. But, shortly before the contract was scheduled to be signed, Aschenbrenner reversed course and announced that he was keeping the Anthropic stake. Instead, he was selling the bulk of his public-stock portfolio—Sandisk and all—to Citadel, Griffin’s hedge fund, at a ten-per-cent discount to market prices. After the transaction was completed, Situational Awareness informed its investors that, in the month of July, it had lost an estimated thirty billion dollars—the single biggest drawdown in hedge-fund history.Just a day later, on August 1st, Aschenbrenner got married. He and Balwit had been planning their wedding for months—the theme was “European Garden, except on the verge of the singularity.” The event was preceded by a small conference on topics including the future of A.I., complete with lightning rounds and breakout sessions. “Debating what will happen in the future is our job,” Aschenbrenner said, of his and Balwit’s friends. “It’s also all of our main hobby.” The ceremony took place at an estate in Carmel Valley, with about a hundred and fifty guests in attendance; Ross Douthat, then an opinion columnist for the Times, was the officiant. (Douthat had befriended Aschenbrenner after reading “Situational Awareness.”) Dwarkesh Patel, one of the groomsmen, was surprised by how unaffected Aschenbrenner seemed by the previous week’s events. Aschenbrenner is a remarkably resilient person, he told me—he hadn’t seemed affected when he’d been fired by OpenAI, either. Later, at the reception, Patel gave a toast. “Leopold was supposed to find an engagement ring worth three months’ salary, but he couldn’t find anything that big,” he said. Referring to the hedge fund’s reversal, he quipped,“So he found another way to show her how much she means to him.”In the aftermath of the liquidation, Falk-Wallace, who now runs a software company called Arcana, decided to reconstruct Situational Awareness’s portfolio, using a combination of public filings, Aschenbrenner’s statements, and a little guesswork. He found that Aschenbrenner was an excellent stock picker. “The hard thing to do in the A.I. thesis was predicting what part of the supply chain would be the next narrative that everyone would freak out about,” Falk-Wallace told me. “He nailed that.”But Situational Awareness also took on more risk than any hedge fund Falk-Wallace had ever seen. Such funds can “hedge” exposure by balancing long positions against short ones. The resulting risk is sometimes calculated using a measure called “vol,” or implied volatility. The typical fund runs at about five per cent vol; a very aggressive fund might run at thirty. Situational Awareness, he estimated, was somewhere close to a hundred per cent. Plus, the hardware and software trades were inversely correlated, meaning that, if one side of the portfolio failed, the other side probably would, too. “He wasn’t truly hedged at all,” Falk-Wallace said.My meeting with Aschenbrenner took place shortly after he returned from his honeymoon to Italy. “My wife is great,” Aschenbrenner said, smiling. “We went to the Dolomites. You know, the German-speaking part.” He did not discuss details of the blowup with me, but his confidence in his central ideas was unshaken. “ ‘Situational Awareness’ was wrong in a number of respects,” he said, referring to the essay. “But, uniformly, when I was wrong, it was because things have gone faster than I expected.”Despite suffering one of the largest dollar-value wipeouts in recent history, Situational Awareness remains a profitable investment for most of Aschenbrenner’s backers, and still has more than ten billion dollars under management. Its offices were busy the day I visited, with many of its twenty-odd employees on the trading floor. In addition to holding on to the Anthropic stake, Situational Awareness had restarted trading in the stock market. Aschenbrenner had cut back on leverage, but kept betting on Sandisk.Blowing up can be a rite of passage for a hedge-fund manager. (Griffin, who bailed Aschenbrenner out, posted a fifty-five-per-cent loss in his flagship fund in 2008.) But the trades Aschenbrenner leans toward have continued to go in the wrong direction. Sandisk’s share price is now lower than when Aschenbrenner was forced to sell it the first time. Nvidia, the engine of the A.I.-infrastructure trade, has seen its share price drop more than thirty per cent from its peak, following the resignation of its C.E.O., Jensen Huang, who had affairs with multiple women, including an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. (China denies that she is a spy.) The scandal has dragged down the “neocloud” data-center stocks Aschenbrenner favors, which rely on Nvidia for financing. Meanwhile, Accenture’s stock price has continued to climb, and the company posted record earnings in October.Rather than approaching ten per cent, G.D.P. growth for this year looks like it will come in at around three. A.I. hasn’t yet resulted in mass job losses: unemployment figures are stable at around four per cent. In August, an analysis of survey data found that about two-fifths of U.S. workers reported using A.I. on the job—but, when they were asked how much of their time this saved them, they estimated two per cent. Right now, the market seems to expect that A.I. will be a technology not unlike railroads or the internet—important, but not cosmic.Hedge funds, for the first time in years, are betting against A.I.
